new_statements.quote: p. 39: "In the following sections I will argue that Barupu has penultimate stress and exemplifies a type of pitch accent system in which, for the majority of words, lexically specified tones are predictably attracted to the stressed syllable and then part or whole of the tone spreads one syllable to the right." p. 50: "That stress is predictably penultimate can be shown by its behaviour on suffixing verbs." p. 51: "That is, stress assignment is not normally weight-sensitive but a closed syllable can satisfy the requirements of the foot when it is the result of this morpho-phonological process." p. 52: "As described above, stress is found on the penultimate syllable of the word and contour tones are assigned to stressed syllables and whole or part of the tone spreads right. ... i build a left-headed, binary foot at the right edge of the word"

new_statements.rule_in_words: Barupu is a word-tone language (five lexical tone classes L, H, LH, HL, HLH) with predictable, non-contrastive stress on the penultimate syllable of the word: a left-headed binary foot is built at the right edge of the word (only the final two syllables are footed, so trisyllables and longer words stress the penult). The lexical tone melody docks on the stressed penult and its last tone spreads one syllable rightwards, giving a pitch-accent-like system. Stress is not weight-sensitive in monomorphemic words (final glide- or nasal-closed syllables do not attract it), but when suffix desyllabification or high-vowel deletion creates a closed final syllable, that syllable satisfies the foot and stress does not shift to the new penult (e.g. /k-a-te-i/ -> [kà.'tej], /k-a-te-ni/ -> [kà.'ten]). Stress is diagnosed phonetically by the slightly higher F0 and longer duration of the penult in L-class words (pp. 48-50), and by the mobility of rule-assigned tones under suffixation (pp. 50-57). The inflected word (prefixes + root + suffixes) is the stress domain; stress can fall on a prefix when the root desyllabifies (/k-a-te-a/ -> ['kà.tʃà], p. 51).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned anywhere in the thesis (grep for 'secondary' finds nothing); syllables other than the final two are described as 'always very short' (p. 49).
new_statements.exceptions: (1) A subset of words have an H or HL lexically linked to the penultimate or the final syllable ('lexically assigned' tones, surface melodies [H.L], [L.H], [L.HL]); these tones do not move with stress under suffixation (pp. 53-57). The lexically assigned final HL is explicitly noted as the exception to contour tones sitting on the stressed syllable (p. 50). (2) Morphophonological closed final syllables satisfy the foot so stress does not reassign (p. 51). (3) Some participant-adding suffixes carry their own tone and show sandhi with hosts (p. 39; §2.4.7). No mention of loanword exceptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: the domain is the inflected phonological word including subject/mood prefixes and object suffixes (verbs) or the noun; examples are citation forms and elicited verb paradigms with F0 traces of single words. The thesis also notes tone interactions in compounds and phrases (§2.4.9) but gives no phrase-level stress rule. Stress is analysed as predictable and non-contrastive; the language is primarily tonal.
new_statements.identity_note: Corris 2005 describes the language of Barupu (formerly Warapu) village, which speakers officially call 'Bauni' (thesis p. 1); this is exactly Glottolog wara1302 'Bauni' (ISO bpe). Miller 2017 (LLM 35) later split the old ISO [wra] 'Warapu' into Bauni (Barupu/Pou villages), Uni (Ramo) and Bouni (Sumo); Corris's data are Bauni proper, from the main Barupu village site after the 1998 tsunami relocation. The thesis header on the repository says 2008 but the document itself is dated 2005 (Wikipedia editor note; the front matter fetched sources here carries no other date).

sources.citation: Miller, Steve A. 2017. Skou languages near Sissano Lagoon, Papua New Guinea. Language and Linguistics in Melanesia 35: 1-24.
sources.note: Language-survey paper (intelligibility, cognate percentages) splitting 'Warapu' into Bauni, Uni, Bouni. No stress statement; only remark on prosody is p. 14: 'Phonetically, Uni has at least two tones, high and low, and the tones contrast phonemically. Bauni has more.' The appendix wordlists (pp. 15-24) carry IPA stress marks (ˈ) on Bauni forms, mostly on the penult but not uniformly (e.g. ˈto.pa vs to.ˈpá 'stone', ni.ˈtú 'green coconut') and the author does not discuss them. The original langlxmelanesia.com URL is dead (HTTP 400); fetched sources from the Wayback capture of 2020-07-12.
